readings.title: A meal rota for new parents
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Neighbours offered meals to a family with a newborn child. Good intentions led to several deliveries on the same evening. The main obstacle was help arriving at inconvenient times. The family had limited refrigerator space and did not want visitors every day. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a private discussion about useful support. One coordinator asked the parents what help they wanted and what information could be shared. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated fewer planned deliveries were more valuable. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a weekly rota with clear boundaries. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: support should follow the recipients wishes. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a meal rota for new parents, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A shared journey to a clinic
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Several residents needed transport to a distant clinic. Volunteers could drive, but appointment times changed at short notice. The main obstacle was a fixed driving timetable that missed visits. People either arrived much too early or cancelled when a volunteer became unavailable. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a review of booking patterns. The group recorded lead times and consulted the clinic about ordinary appointment windows. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated a flexible pool worked better than assigned days. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced advance requests with a backup driver. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: community help needs dependable coordination. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in a shared journey to a clinic, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Welcoming a new neighbour
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An apartment building prepared an information pack for newcomers. Residents liked the gesture but found many printed phone numbers outdated. The main obstacle was contact details that quickly changed. A full booklet had been printed once and was not revised when local services moved. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a check of frequently used contacts. Volunteers called service desks and asked new residents which details they had actually needed. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated a few reliable contacts mattered most. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a short printed guide with a dated online update. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: welcome information must stay current. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in welcoming a new neighbour, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Keeping a toy library useful
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A community centre lent toys to families. Shelves were full, but parents struggled to find items suitable for younger children. The main obstacle was toys organised only by donation date. Boxes mixed small pieces with larger equipment, making choice difficult for caregivers. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used borrowing records and parent feedback. Staff checked ages, safety guidance and the kinds of toys families requested. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated age-based categories improved choice. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced clear labels and regular condition checks. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: shared resources need careful organisation. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in keeping a toy library useful, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
When a community changes the community support network, a short explanation can be as important as the change itself. People want to know what problem was noticed, how information was gathered and why one option was selected. For a project about families and community support, staff observed actual use rather than relying only on a drawing or an early promise. The evidence revealed an obstacle that was not obvious at first. Organizers made a limited adjustment and told residents when it would be reviewed. They also described the limits of the trial, because a small number of visits cannot represent every future situation. An honest account made the decision easier to question and improve.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 社区调整一项服务时，简短解释可能和改动本身同样重要。人们想知道发现了什么问题、如何收集信息，以及为何选择某个方案。在一个有关家庭与社区互助的项目中，工作人员观察实际使用，而不只依靠图纸或最初的承诺。证据揭示了起初并不明显的障碍。组织者作出有限调整，并告知居民何时重新评估。他们也说明试行的局限，因为少量使用经历不能代表未来所有情况。诚实的说明让这项决定更容易被讨论和改进。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the neighbourhood support group suggesting a practical change to the community support network. Describe who should be consulted, how the change could be tried, and when it should be reviewed.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the community support network. People have noticed help arriving at inconvenient times, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
